I can copy a segment and draw a circle with compass and straightedge.

slides.title: Get started
slides.html:
Push a pencil upright through a sheet of paper on a sunny sill, and draw a circle around it with your compass. In the morning, mark where the tip of the shadow touches the circle. In the afternoon, mark where it touches the circle again. Both marks are one radius from the pencil. Which direction is exactly halfway between them?

  • I can copy a segment and draw a circle with compass and straightedge.
  • I can copy a segment with a compass, without measuring.
  • I can construct an equilateral triangle (Euclid I.1) and say why its sides are equal.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: A construction uses only a compass and a straightedge. The straightedge draws a line through two points. The compass draws a circle, and every point on a circle is the same distance from its center. That is how a compass copies a length with no numbers.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: A construction uses only a compass and a straightedge. The straightedge draws a line through two points. The compass draws a circle, and every point on a circle is the same distance from its center. That is how a compass copies a length with no numbers.

slides.title: Words to know
slides.html:
• construction A drawing made with only a compass and a straightedge.
  • compass A tool for drawing circles and copying lengths.
  • straightedge A ruler with no marks, used only to draw straight lines.
  • circle All the points in a plane the same distance from one center point.
  • center The fixed point every point of the circle is the same distance from.
  • radius The distance from the center to the circle, or a segment with that length.
  • arc A piece of a circle between two points on it.

  • arc A piece of a circle between two points on it.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Copy a segment of length 3.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Put the compass points on A and B. Now the opening is 3.The opening matches segment AB.
Keep the opening. Put the point on P and draw an arc across the ray.Same opening, new center.
Call the crossing point Q.Use the crossing on the ray we were given.
Q is on a circle with center P and radius 3, so PQ = 3.Every point on a circle is one radius from the center.
Second check: we never read a ruler. The circle rule alone gives PQ = 3.That is what makes it a construction.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Find the mistake: the opening changed.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
A student sets the compass to AB, which is 4.Good start.
Then the student changes the opening to 6 before drawing at P.This is the error.
The new circle has radius 6, so the copy is 6, not 4.The copy equals the opening you draw with.
Fix: keep the opening exactly the same when you move the compass to P.Then the radius still equals AB.

geo.title: Worked example
geo.prompt: Find the mistake: the opening changed.

steps.step: A student sets the compass to AB, which is 4.
Then the student changes the opening to 6 before drawing at P.
The new circle has radius 6, so the copy is 6, not 4.
steps.reason: The copy equals the opening you draw with.

steps.step: Fix: keep the opening exactly the same when you move the compass to P.
steps.reason: Then the radius still equals AB.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Ty says 'a compass is only for drawing circles.'

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

A compass can hold and transfer a length, not just draw circles. Set its tips to the endpoints of a source segment, then move it without changing the opening. The distance between the tips is still the source length. Opening or closing the compass changes that stored length. No ruler reading or numerical measurement is required.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
You have two segments with lengths a and b, where a > b > 0. Using only a compass and straightedge, place T on a given ray from P so that PT + b = a. You may use two stated rules. First rule: if T is between P and Q, then PT + TQ = PQ. Second rule: a circle centered at one end of a segment, with radius more than 0 but less than the segment's length, crosses the segment at exactly one point inside it. Don't read a ruler.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Copy a from P along the ray to get Q, so PQ = a. Reset the compass to the second source segment, whose length is b. Keep this new opening unchanged while moving the compass point to Q, then draw the circle centered at Q. Choose its intersection T strictly between P and Q, not the intersection past Q. Then TQ = b, because T is on the circle. The first rule gives PT + b = PT + TQ = PQ = a. The second rule says this T exists, because b is more than 0 and less than a.

Reveal second check

Number-line check: put P at 0 and Q at a. The circle crosses the line at a - b and a + b, and only a - b is between 0 and a. With a = 9 and b = 4, T = 5 works, since 5 + 4 = 9. The other point, 13, does not.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
You draw a full circle with center P and radius AB, and a ray from P going right. The circle meets the line through the ray in two places. Which one is the copied endpoint? Is the other one on the ray?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Use Q, the crossing on the ray. PQ = AB by the circle rule. R is on the opposite ray, going left, so it is not on our ray.

Reveal second check

The ray picks the direction. The full line has two crossings, but only one is on the ray.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
Circle O has radius r. U and V are on the circle. W is a point, but we don't know where. Which must be true: OU = OV, OU = OW, or UV = r?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Only OU = OV, since both equal r. W might not be on the circle, and UV does not have to be a radius.

Reveal second check

Put W at O: then OW is zero, not r. Put U and V straight across from each other: then UV = 2r, not r.
